introduction-the-cpu-trap.core: CPU-based autoscaling is a lagging, indirect signal: a queue worker waiting on I/O shows low CPU while thousands of messages pile up, and idle services can't scale to zero. Event-driven autoscaling scales on the actual work signal (queue depth, stream lag, request rate, cron schedules) and can drop to zero replicas when there's nothing to do.

first_principles.problem: A Kafka consumer group falls hours behind because HPA sees 15% CPU and doesn't scale.
derivation: Allow **scale to zero** for event workloads.

analogy.title: Staffing a checkout by queue length, not by how tired cashiers look
analogy.story: Long queue, open more tills, however relaxed the cashiers seem.
analogy.breaks: Queues are visible at a glance; external metrics need scalers to fetch them.

example.title: Lag vs CPU
flow: Kafka lag 2M → KEDA: scale to 30 consumers

check.q: Why is CPU a poor scaling signal for queue consumers?
check.a: They may be I/O-bound with low CPU while backlog grows, so CPU doesn't reflect demand.

keda-architecture-the-metrics-proxy.core: KEDA runs an operator and a metrics API server. The operator watches ScaledObjects, handles 0↔1 activation itself (scaling Deployments to zero and back) and creates an HPA for 1↔N. The metrics server exposes external metrics fetched by 60+ scalers (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ, Prometheus, Redis, cron, HTTP) to that HPA.

first_principles.problem: HPA alone can't read SQS queue depth or scale to zero.
truths: Zero replicas means no Pods to report metrics.

analogy.title: A dispatcher with a phone line to every warehouse
analogy.story: It checks stock levels everywhere and tells the staffing manager how many workers to send.
analogy.breaks: Dispatchers wake staff from home; KEDA must still wait for Pods to start from zero.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: KEDA-managed HPA driven by external metrics.

code.text:
kubectl get scaledobject -n workers
kubectl get hpa -n workers        # keda-hpa-orders-consumer
kubectl get --raw /apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 | jq

check.q: Which component scales a workload from 0 to 1 replicas in KEDA?
check.a: The KEDA operator itself (HPA handles 1 to N).

the-magic-of-scale-to-zero.core: When a trigger reports no activity (below activation threshold) for the cooldownPeriod, KEDA scales the Deployment to zero, eliminating idle cost. When events appear, KEDA activates it to one replica and HPA scales further. Trade-offs: cold-start latency, polling intervals delaying reaction, and the need for an external buffer (queue) so events aren't lost while scaled down.

first_principles.problem: Dozens of rarely used workers each run 2 replicas around the clock.
truths: Buffers hold work while scaled down.
derivation: Ensure events sit in a **durable queue**.

analogy.title: Lights on motion sensors
analogy.story: They switch off in empty rooms and on when someone enters, with a brief delay.
analogy.breaks: Lights react instantly; KEDA polls on an interval and Pods take seconds to start.

example.title: Nightly-only worker
flow: Batch messages arrive → activate within 30 s

check.q: Why must scale-to-zero workloads read from a durable queue?
check.a: Events must be held safely while no consumers are running.

the-custom-resource-scaledobject.core: A ScaledObject targets a Deployment or StatefulSet (scaleTargetRef) and defines triggers (type plus metadata like queue URL and target value), min and max replicas, polling and cooldown, fallback replicas if the scaler fails, and advanced HPA behaviour. ScaledJob instead launches Jobs per batch of events for long-running tasks.

first_principles.problem: A team wants consumers that scale with SQS depth, one replica per 100 messages.
truths: Targets per replica define desired count.
Long tasks fit Jobs better than Deployments.

analogy.title: A rule card for the staffing manager
analogy.story: 'One worker per 100 waiting parcels, at least zero, at most 50.'
analogy.breaks: Rule cards are read by people; ScaledObjects are reconciled continuously.

check.q: What does the fallback section in a ScaledObject do?
check.a: Sets a fixed replica count if the scaler fails repeatedly to fetch metrics.

authentication-triggerauthentication.core: Scalers need credentials to read queues and metrics. TriggerAuthentication (namespaced) and ClusterTriggerAuthentication reference secrets, environment variables or pod identity providers (AWS IRSA/EKS Pod Identity, Azure Workload Identity, GCP Workload Identity) and Vault, so credentials aren't embedded in ScaledObjects.

first_principles.problem: Queue credentials are pasted into ScaledObject metadata in Git.
truths: Credentials must not live in manifests.
Many ScaledObjects reuse the same auth.

analogy.title: A staff badge office
analogy.story: Dispatchers don't carry keys; they show the badge office's authorisation when checking warehouses.
analogy.breaks: Badges are physical; misconfigured identity silently stops scaling.

code.text:
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata: {name: aws-irsa, namespace: workers}
spec:
  podIdentity:
    provider: aws
    identityOwner: keda   # KEDA operator's service account role

check.q: Why use TriggerAuthentication instead of putting credentials in a ScaledObject?
check.a: It keeps secrets out of manifests, enables reuse and supports workload identity.
